section.title: Flee Idolatry, Do All to God's Glory
section.sectionRationale: Paul brings the whole discussion of idol food to its point. Because the Lord's Supper is a real participation in the blood and body of Christ, and because the one loaf makes the many one body, believers cannot also share the table of demons. From this he draws the pastoral resolution: freedom is real, but it must be governed by love that seeks the good of others and by a single aim, the glory of God. Whether eating, drinking, or anything else, do all to God's glory, giving no offense, seeking the salvation of many, imitating Paul as he imitates Christ.
section.thesis: Because the cup and the bread are a participation in the blood and body of Christ, and the one loaf makes the many one body, believers must flee idolatry and cannot share the table of demons; and since everything is to be done for the glory of God, freedom is to be ruled by love that seeks the good and salvation of many, imitating Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: flee idolatry because the Supper is a real sharing in Christ and makes one body; the impossibility of sharing the Lord's table and the table of demons; freedom governed by love that seeks the good of others; and the summit, do all to the glory of God, giving no offense and imitating Christ.

units.label: Flee idolatry, one loaf one body

verses.text: Therefore, my beloved, flee from {{eidololatria|idolatry}}.
I speak to reasonable people; judge for yourselves what I say.
Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a {{koinonia|participation}} in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?
Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf.
Consider the people of Israel: Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?
Am I suggesting, then, that food sacrificed to an idol is anything, or that an idol is anything?
No, but the sacrifices of pagans are offered to {{daimonion|demons}}, not to God. And I do not want you to be participants with demons.
You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too; you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too.
Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?
“Everything is permissible,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible,” but not everything is edifying.
No one should seek his own good, but the good of others.
Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience,
for, “The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”
If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat anything set before you without raising questions of conscience.
But if someone tells you, “This food was offered to idols,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience,
the other one’s conscience, I mean, not your own. For why should my freedom be determined by someone else’s conscience?
If I partake in the meal with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?
So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the {{doxa|glory}} of God.
Do not become a stumbling block, whether to Jews or Greeks or the church of God,
as I also try to please everyone in all I do. For I am not seeking my own good, but the good of many, that they may be saved.
You are to imitate me, just as I {{mimeomai|imitate}} Christ.

eidololatria.gloss: Idolatry, the worship or service of images. Paul commands the church to flee it, not to test how near they can stand. Because the living God will share His people with no rival, idolatry is not a harmless custom but a betrayal that provokes the Lord's jealousy.

koinonia.gloss: Participation, communion, a real sharing in common. The cup and the bread are a koinonia in the blood and body of Christ, a genuine joining to Him and to one another, not a bare symbol. It is the theological engine of the passage: because the Supper truly unites us to Christ, we cannot also unite ourselves to demons at their table.

daimonion.gloss: A demon, an evil spirit. An idol is nothing, yet the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons behind the images. To share a pagan sacrificial meal is to become a participant with demons, which is why the two tables are utterly incompatible.

doxa.gloss: Glory, weight, honor, the manifest worth of God. The whole ethic of freedom is gathered under one aim: whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God. It reframes eating, drinking, and every ordinary act as an opportunity to display and honor the worth of God.

mimeomai.gloss: To imitate, to follow as a model. Paul calls the church to imitate him only insofar as he imitates Christ, so the chain of discipleship leads always back to the Lord. The self-denying, others-seeking freedom he has described is finally the shape of Christ's own life.

basic.context: Paul finishes the long discussion about food offered to idols with a clear command and a soaring principle. The command is simple: flee idolatry. He explains why with the Lord's Supper. When the church shares the cup and the bread, it is really sharing in the blood and body of Christ, and the one loaf makes the many into one body. That kind of real sharing cannot be mixed with the pagan sacrificial meals, because behind the idols are demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. Then he answers practical questions about buying meat and eating at a neighbor's house: use your freedom, but always for the good of others and, above all, for the glory of God. Whatever you do, do it all to God's glory, seeking the salvation of many, following Paul as he follows Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul distinguishes carefully. An idol is nothing, and meat is just meat, so ordinary market food may be eaten freely with thanksgiving. But deliberate participation in idol worship is spiritual treason, because it joins a person to demons and provokes God's jealousy. The governing rules are love, which seeks the good of others and refuses to be a stumbling block, and God's glory, which is the aim of every act. Verse 31 lifts a debate about food into a rule for the whole of life.
basic.originalLanguages: The section opens with a command to flee eidololatria, idolatry. Its reason is koinonia: the cup and bread are a real participation in the blood and body of Christ. Behind pagan sacrifices stand daimonion, demons, so the two tables cannot be shared. The whole matter is then gathered under one word, doxa, glory: do it all to the glory of God. And the pattern is set by mimeomai, imitation, following Paul as he follows Christ.
basic.typology: Israel's sacrificial meals, where those who ate the offerings shared in the altar, are the pattern Paul uses to explain the Lord's Supper: eating at a table joins you to what the table serves. The Passover and fellowship offerings that made worshippers partakers in the altar find their fulfillment in the Supper, where believers share in Christ, our Passover, once for all sacrificed.
basic.christ: The center of this passage is the Lord's Supper as a real sharing in the crucified and risen Christ. His shed blood and given body are the church's true food, and communion with Him is so real that it makes many people one body and rules out communion with demons. The closing verse names Him as the final model: Paul's self-giving freedom, and the church's, is simply the imitation of Christ, who sought not His own good but ours, that we might be saved.
basic.god: God is jealous for His people with a holy jealousy; to flirt with idols is to provoke the Lord, and we are not stronger than He. Yet He is also the generous Creator: the earth is the Lord's and everything in it, so His people may eat with thanksgiving. Above all He is the God whose glory is the goal of every action, the one whose worth we display when we lay down our rights to seek the good and salvation of others.
basic.crossReferences: The Gospels record Jesus giving the cup and the bread as His blood and body. Deuteronomy warns that Israel's sacrifices to demons provoke God's jealousy. The Psalms declare the earth is the Lord's and its fullness. Philippians calls the church to look to the interests of others as Christ did.
basic.oneStory: From Eden onward the great human failure has been idolatry, giving to created things the worship owed to God, and the great rescue is a people reconciled to worship Him alone. Here the church, joined to Christ at His table, is called out of idolatry into a life whose single aim is God's glory. In seeking the good and salvation of many rather than their own, believers imitate Christ and take their place in the story that ends with every knee bowing to Him.

context.literary:
This is the third and last panel of the long answer about idol food that began in chapter 8. Chapter 8 argued from love, chapter 9 from Paul's own example, and chapter 10 first from Israel's history and now, from verse 14, from the nature of worship itself. The paragraph division at 11:1 is unfortunate, because 11:1 is the last line of this argument and belongs with it: 'imitate me, just as I imitate Christ.' The section is a single movement with four stages.

Verses 14 to 17 give the command and its first ground, the Lord's Supper. Verses 18 to 22 widen the evidence with Israel's altar and with the demonic reality behind pagan sacrifice, and end with a pair of sharp questions. Verses 23 to 30 turn to practical cases, using what many take to be quotations from the Corinthians, 'Everything is permissible,' and showing how love and conscience limit them. Verses 31 to 11:1 gather it into one rule, the glory of God, and one pattern, Christ.

The style changes with the stages. Verses 15 to 22 rely on questions that expect the answer yes, so the reader is led to the conclusion rather than told. Verses 25 to 30 shift to short rulings with their reasons. Verse 31 is a single sentence that sums up three chapters, and it takes the form of a universal, 'whether you eat or drink or whatever you do.' The shape is a funnel, from a firm command through careful case work to one governing principle.
context.historical:
The Lord's Supper at Corinth was not yet a small ritual. It was part of a shared meal, as 11:17-34 shows, and the Corinthians would have placed it in a world where meals were the setting for religious loyalty. To eat at a table was to be joined to the host, and to eat at a god's table was to be joined to the god. That is why Paul can argue from one table to another.

Pagan sacrificial dinners took place in the temple precincts, and these banquets were part of civic and social life. A person who declined risked offence to a patron or a business partner. Many ordinary people also bought meat in the market, which in Latin was the macellum, and some of that meat had come from sacrifice while some had not. Paul's rulings in verses 25 to 30 show that he knew the market was full of such meat and that he would not have believers search it for its history.

The Old Testament background is Israel's sacrificial system, where those who ate the offerings had a share in the altar, Leviticus 7:15-18, and the Song of Moses, which charges Israel with sacrificing to demons and provoking God's jealousy, Deuteronomy 32:16-17. The Greek and Roman world had its own accounts of spirits and powers behind its worship, and Paul's claim that demons stand behind pagan sacrifice would have sounded to them like a serious spiritual claim, not a metaphor.
context.canonical:
The most direct background is Deuteronomy 32, where Moses says Israel provoked God's jealousy with foreign gods and sacrificed to demons, not to God, Deuteronomy 32:16-17. Paul's phrase in verse 20 is close to the wording of that passage, and his question in verse 22, 'Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?', echoes verse 21 of the same chapter. Psalm 106:37 also speaks of sacrifices to demons, and Leviticus 17:7 forbade sacrifices to the goat demons.

The cup and the bread go back to the upper room, where Jesus gave them as His blood and body, Matthew 26:26-28, and Paul repeats the tradition in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26. The 'one loaf' recalls the unity of the body that Paul describes in 12:12-13 and in Ephesians 4:4-6. The Passover lies behind it all, since Christ is called our Passover lamb in 1 Corinthians 5:7.

Verse 26 quotes Psalm 24:1, 'The earth is the LORD's, and the fullness thereof,' and verse 31 has a close companion in Colossians 3:17, 'whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus.' Romans 14:6-8 and Romans 12:1 develop the same thought, that the whole of life is offered to God. Verse 33's 'seeking not my own good but the good of many' matches Philippians 2:4, and 11:1 prepares for Ephesians 5:1-2, which calls believers to imitate God and walk in love as Christ loved us.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted to remove any ground for believers to think that idol feasts were harmless. He had agreed that an idol is nothing, and he did not take that back. What he adds is that the practice of worship involves real spiritual powers, and a believer cannot belong to two tables. The Corinthians' clever reasoning had left out the demonic reality, and Paul puts it back.

He also wanted to keep them from the opposite error, a fussy scrupulosity that checks every piece of meat. In verses 25 to 30 he gives a plain rule for ordinary life. Eat what is put before you and ask no questions, unless someone makes the origin of the food an issue, and then refrain for the sake of that person's conscience. The point is that freedom is real and love is real, and neither cancels the other.

And he wanted the whole discussion lifted into a single aim. The question 'May I?' gives way to 'Will this glorify God, and will it do good to others?' Verse 31 is not an addendum to the rules but the key to them, and 11:1 gives that aim a face: Paul's own life, which in turn imitates Christ.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes meals and markets in a pagan city, and it prescribes responses to them. The specific commands, to flee idolatry, to avoid the table of demons, to eat what is sold in the market without raising questions, and to refrain when told the food was offered to an idol, are bound to a setting in which meat and temple were closely linked. Most believers today do not meet that exact situation.

The principle carries across. Idolatry is still worship of anything that takes God's place, and believers are still told to flee it. The Lord's Supper is still a participation in Christ. The rule for disputed matters is still that freedom is shaped by the good of others and the glory of God. Paul's closing command, to imitate him as he imitates Christ, is not an invitation to copy his every habit. It is an invitation to follow the pattern of his life, which is the pattern of Christ's self giving.

A further caution is to avoid reading the Corinthian slogans as Paul's own teaching. 'Everything is permissible' is a claim he quotes and qualifies. It is true in its limited sense, and false when treated as the last word.

debates.question: What does it mean that the cup and bread are a 'participation' in the blood and body of Christ?

views.label: A real presence of Christ in the elements
views.case: Catholic and Lutheran teaching reads Paul's words as strongly as they will go. The cup is a participation in the blood, and the bread in the body, because Christ is truly present in or under the elements. They point to the parallel with the table of demons, which they say involves a real association.

views.label: A real spiritual communion with the risen Christ
views.case: Reformed teaching, following Calvin, holds that believers truly receive Christ by the Spirit as they eat in faith, though Christ's body is in heaven. The participation is real and spiritual, and the parallel with demons is a parallel of fellowship and not of physical presence.

views.label: A memorial and a pledge of loyalty
views.case: Another tradition, associated with Zwingli, stresses remembrance and the public declaration of allegiance, 11:24-26. The meal binds the community to Christ in a vow, as the pagan meal binds worshippers to the god.

debates.bearing: All three agree on what Paul's argument needs: the Supper is a binding act of fellowship with Christ, so that it excludes a rival fellowship. The differences concern the manner of the presence, which Paul does not explain here.

debates.question: Who is the person who says, 'This food was offered to idols,' in verse 28?

views.label: A weak Christian
views.case: Paul speaks of conscience, and the person who raises the issue is likely a fellow believer who is troubled. This fits chapter 8, where the weak brother is wounded when he sees the strong eat. On this reading Paul asks the strong to refrain for that person's sake.

views.label: An unbelieving host or guest
views.case: The word used for the food here, which is not the usual one, is the neutral word a pagan would use, and it points to a non Christian. If so, the abstaining is a witness: it makes clear that the believer does not share the pagan reading of the meal, and it avoids giving the impression that idolatry is of no account.

debates.bearing: The ruling is the same either way. When the food's religious meaning is made explicit, the believer declines, out of concern for the other person's conscience and for the clarity of the believer's own witness.

study.originalLanguages:
The command in verse 14 is pheugete, 'flee,' a present imperative that means to keep fleeing. Paul used the same verb for sexual immorality in 6:18, and he uses it for the love of money and for youthful passions in 1 Timothy 6:11 and 2 Timothy 2:22. Idolatry is something to run from, and not a thing to be argued with. Paul adds 'my beloved' and 'to sensible people,' phronimois, in verse 15, which invites them to weigh the argument with the minds they have.

The cup is called 'the cup of blessing,' to poterion tes eulogias, a phrase that matches the name of the blessing pronounced over the cup at the Jewish meal. The noun koinonia, 'participation' or 'sharing,' stands at the heart of the passage, and Paul builds a family of words around it: koinonoi, 'partners,' in verses 18 and 20, and metecho, 'to partake,' in verses 17 and 21. The point is of association: the table makes partners. The 'one loaf' of verse 17 explains how many people are one body, because they all share in one bread.

In verse 20 Paul says the sacrifices are offered to daimonia, 'demons,' and not to God. The wording is close to that of the Greek translation of Deuteronomy 32:17, so Paul is quoting the Song of Moses and not inventing a new idea. In verse 22 the verb is parazeloo, to provoke to jealousy, which is the verb of the Greek version of Deuteronomy 32:21.

Verse 23 repeats 'Everything is permissible,' panta exestin, which many take as a Corinthian slogan, and Paul answers with two words. 'Beneficial' is sympherei, what brings together to profit, and 'edifying' is oikodomei, what builds. The market in verse 25 is the makellon, a Latin loan word macellum, meat market. In verse 28 the food is called hierothyton, 'offered in sacrifice,' a word that appears only here in the New Testament, whereas Paul has used eidolothyton elsewhere. The new word is the more neutral one that a pagan might use, which may mean the speaker was not a Christian.

The word 'conscience,' syneidesis, occurs three times in verses 25 to 29. The final sentence in verse 31 is eis doxan theou poieite, 'do for the glory of God,' with a present imperative, so the command is to go on doing all things this way. Verse 32 uses aproskopoi, 'without offense,' and verse 33 sets 'my own good' against 'the good of many.' The last word, mimetai, 'imitators,' gives the English word 'mimic,' though Paul means a following of character rather than a copy of behavior.

typology.type: The shared altar of Israel, 1 Corinthians 10:18
typology.fulfillment: Those who ate Israel's sacrifices shared in the altar, Leviticus 7:15-18, and Paul draws on this to explain what happens at the Lord's table. The correspondence is that eating together binds the eaters to the one the table honors. In Christ the altar is the cross, and those who eat the bread and cup share in what was done there. The type falls short in one respect: Israel's worshippers shared in an altar that had to be served over and over, while believers share in a sacrifice that was made once for all, Hebrews 10:10-14.

Israel ate the Passover lamb in each household, and the meal bound them as a people who had been rescued, Exodus 12:3-14. Paul says that Christ is our Passover lamb, 1 Corinthians 5:7, and the Supper takes its form from that meal, since Jesus gave the cup and bread at a Passover table, Luke 22:14-20. The correspondence is of a rescue celebrated by a meal. The escalation is that the Lamb is Christ and the rescue is from sin and death. It falls short as a type because the yearly lamb looked ahead, and the Supper looks back to the cross and forward to the feast of the kingdom.

typology.type: The one loaf and the one body, 1 Corinthians 10:17
typology.fulfillment: Many grains make one loaf, and many believers make one body. The picture works because bread is a shared substance and a shared act. In Christ the body is His own, the church, Ephesians 4:4-6, and the unity is created by sharing in Him. The type falls short in that bread is a passive thing, while the church is a living body animated by the Spirit, 1 Corinthians 12:13, and it must still be guarded against divisions, as 11:18 shows.

study.christ:
The Supper puts Christ in the room. Paul calls the cup 'a participation in the blood of Christ' and the bread 'a participation in the body of Christ,' verse 16. Whatever one's view of the manner of His presence, to eat and drink here is to meet the Lord who died, and to be tied to Him as He now lives.

That is why the passage can say that the Lord's table excludes the table of demons. A believer is already bound to Christ by His death, and a second binding is impossible. Paul's argument assumes that Christ is a person with a claim on His people, and that He is jealous for them. The question 'Are we stronger than He?' in verse 22 treats Christ as Lord to whom the church is accountable, and that Lord is the One described in 8:6, through whom all things came.

The passage leads to Christ by the Passover. Christ is called our Passover lamb in 5:7, and the meal Jesus gave at the Passover table is now the church's continuing feast, Luke 22:19-20. The blood is the blood of the covenant, and what Moses sprinkled on the people, Exodus 24:8, Christ gives in a better form.

It leads to Christ in His love for others. Paul says he seeks not his own good but the good of many, 10:33, and then points to Christ as the model, 11:1. The model is the Christ of Romans 15:3 who did not please Himself, and of Philippians 2:4-8. Believers who set aside a freedom for the sake of another are not doing something strange. They are following the One whose whole life was lived for others.

A caution is needed about the Supper. The passage is aimed at those who might treat it as a harmless ritual, and it warns that fellowship at His table has consequences. Paul does not teach that the elements work like magic. The next chapter shows that unworthy participation brings judgment, 11:27-30. The Supper is a gift that calls for faith and for loyalty.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who is jealous. The word has a bad sound in English, but the jealousy of the Lord is the zeal of a faithful husband for a people He has made His own. Exodus 20:5 says He is a jealous God, and Paul's question in verse 22, 'Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?', assumes that He will not share the love and worship of His people. Jealousy of that kind is the opposite of pettiness. It is the response of one who has given everything and who wants the love to be true.

He is also the generous Creator. Paul quotes Psalm 24:1, 'The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof,' to say that the market, the table and the food all belong to God, and that believers may eat without anxiety, and with thanks, verses 26 and 30. The same God who forbids the table of demons gives the whole earth for enjoyment. The two truths belong together: He is jealous for His people and generous to them.

He is the God whose glory is the goal of everything. Verse 31 does not say that eating and drinking are unimportant. It says that even eating and drinking can be done for His glory. That puts the ordinary on the same level as the sacred, and it means that worship is not limited to a building. A God whose glory fills the earth is honored in a meal as in a hymn.

He is holy and has enemies. Paul names the demons plainly. The demonic is real, though it does not turn an idol into a god or meat into poison. God's holiness means that His people may not share a table with those powers, and God's power means that they need not fear them. The believer who flees idolatry runs toward a Lord who is stronger than any rival.

For worship, the passage asks for undivided loyalty, for grateful receiving, and for a life aimed at His glory. It also gives a test for any act: does it honor God, and does it do good to others? The God who is jealous, generous and glorious is the one whom we worship at the table and in the market, and in everything between.

crossReferences.note: Jesus gives the bread as His body and the cup as His blood of the covenant. This is the institution that Paul assumes when he speaks of the cup of blessing and the bread that we break, and it shows that the participation is in a covenant sealed by a death.

Moses says that Israel provoked God to jealousy with foreign gods and sacrificed to demons, not to God. Paul's wording in verse 20 and his question in verse 22 are drawn from this song, and they show that his claim about demons was an old one in Israel.

The rules for the peace offering, a sacrifice that was eaten by the worshipper. It shows that in Israel eating an offering was a form of sharing in the altar, which is the point of Paul's appeal in verse 18.

The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof. Paul quotes it in verse 26 to say that market food is not unclean, since everything belongs to the Creator, and it grounds the freedom to eat with thanks.
Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. It links the Supper to the Passover and explains why Paul can speak of the meal as a real sharing in what Christ did.
Paul's account of the institution of the Supper, with its call to remember and proclaim the Lord's death until He comes. It fills out what the shorter reference in chapter 10 assumes.

You were bought with a price, so glorify God with your body. This is the same aim as 10:31, set in the context of sexual morality, and it shows that the glory of God is the rule for the whole of bodily life.
Whoever eats, eats to the Lord and gives thanks to God, and none of us lives to himself. It gives the same two motives as 1 Corinthians 10:30-33, thanks to God and concern for others.

Whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him. It is a close companion to verse 31, and it adds that the name of Jesus is the form of doing all things to God's glory.

Do nothing out of selfish ambition, and look to the interests of others, having the mind of Christ. It states the principle of verse 24 and verse 33, and it shows that the pattern of 11:1 is the mind that was in Christ Jesus.

study.oneStory:
Idolatry is the root failure of the Bible's story. Romans 1:23-25 says that humanity exchanged the glory of God for images and worshipped the creature in place of the Creator. The golden calf, the high places, the gods of Canaan and the household idols are all chapters in that same exchange. The first commandment, to have no other gods, is the first demand of the covenant, and the prophets spend centuries calling Israel back to it.

Paul's command to flee idolatry stands in that line, and it adds something new. The church now has a table, and the table is Christ's. The meal joins many people from many nations into one body, which is the thing that the old altar could not do. Genesis 12:3 promised that all the families of the earth would be blessed, and a table at which Jew and Gentile eat one loaf is part of the answer.

The passage also sets the aim of redeemed life, the glory of God. Humanity was made to reflect that glory, Genesis 1:26-27, and lost the ability when it turned to other things. The new creation in Christ restores it, so that even eating and drinking are done for God's glory. This is the beginning of a world in which everything is used for its Maker.

It ends in the feast. Jesus said He would not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom came, Matthew 26:29, and Revelation 19:9 speaks of the wedding supper of the Lamb. In the new creation the false gods are gone and the table is one, and the people of God eat at the Lord's table with Him. Until then, the church eats the bread and drinks the cup, flees every rival, and does all things for the glory of God, imitating Christ as Paul did.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say believers cannot share the table of the Lord and the table of demons?

options.text: Because the Supper is a real participation in Christ that cannot be mixed with communion with demons.
options.note: Verses 16 to 21: real sharing in Christ rules out sharing with demons behind the idols.

options.text: Because sharing the pagan table makes one a participant with demons.
options.note: True and stated in verse 20, though the deeper reason is the incompatible communion with Christ at His table.

options.text: Because idols are powerful gods to be feared.
options.note: An idol is nothing, yet demons stand behind pagan sacrifice.

options.text: Because eating any meat is forbidden.
options.note: Paul frees them to eat market meat with thanks; the issue is idol worship.

quiz.q: What does koinonia mean in the phrase a participation in the blood of Christ?

options.text: A real sharing and communion in Christ, not a bare symbol.
options.note: The reality of the sharing is what makes the two tables incompatible.

options.text: A covenant sign that seals our union with Christ, received by faith.
options.note: A faithful reading that still affirms real communion, though it emphasizes the sign rather than the sharing itself.

options.text: A mere reminder with no real connection to Christ.
options.note: Paul's argument depends on a genuine participation.

options.text: A private feeling unrelated to the church.
options.note: The one loaf makes the many one body; it is deeply corporate.

quiz.q: How should believers use their freedom, according to this passage?

options.text: For the good of others and the glory of God, giving no offense.
options.note: Verses 24, 31, and 32 govern freedom by love and God's glory.

options.text: Freely, but only in ways that are beneficial and build others up.
options.note: True to verse 23, though the fullest answer names God's glory and the good of others as the aim.

options.text: However they please, since everything is permissible.
options.note: Permissible, yes, but not everything is beneficial or edifying.

options.text: By avoiding all contact with unbelievers.
options.note: Paul allows dining with unbelievers; the aim is their good and salvation.

quiz.q: What is the overarching principle of verse 31?

options.text: Whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God.
options.note: The whole of life, not just food, is to be lived for God's glory.

options.text: Even ordinary acts like eating and drinking can honor God.
options.note: True and drawn from the verse, though the principle sweeps wider to whatever you do.

options.text: Only religious acts count as glorifying God.
options.note: Even eating and drinking are to glorify God, so the principle covers all of life.

options.text: Avoid food and drink to be holy.
options.note: The point is not abstinence but doing all to God's glory.

quiz.q: Whom does Paul finally point to as the model to imitate?

options.text: Christ, whom Paul himself imitates in seeking the good of many.
options.note: 11:1: imitate me as I imitate Christ; the chain leads back to the Lord.

options.text: Paul, but only as he follows Christ's example.
options.note: Right that Paul is a pattern, though the final model he points to is Christ Himself.

options.text: Paul alone, as the ultimate example.
options.note: Paul is a model only insofar as he imitates Christ.

options.text: The surrounding pagan culture.
options.note: He calls them away from idolatry, not toward the culture.

questions: Paul says flee idolatry, not merely avoid it. What in your life competes with God for your worship, and what would fleeing rather than flirting with it look like?
The Lord's Supper is a real sharing in Christ and unites us as one body. How might a deeper sense of that reality change the way you come to the Lord's table and to your church family?
Everything may be permissible, but not everything is beneficial or edifying. Where do you need to weigh your freedom by love for others rather than by your rights?
Verse 31 makes God's glory the aim of eating, drinking, and everything. Take one ordinary part of your day and ask how it could be done to the glory of God.
Paul sought the good of many that they might be saved, imitating Christ. Whose salvation might God be calling you to seek by laying down some comfort or preference?

translationNotes.note: Participation translates koinonia, a real communion or sharing; the cup and bread genuinely join believers to Christ and to one another, which is why the passage rules out any parallel sharing with demons.
An idol is nothing, yet Paul says pagan sacrifices are offered to demons; the images are empty, but real spiritual powers stand behind idol worship, making it far from harmless.
This verse belongs with the preceding movement, not the next; it seals the argument by pointing beyond Paul to Christ, whom he imitates in seeking the good of many.
